title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 5: Presidential Secrecy
keywords: successor NEDA DG Augusto B. Santos
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's June 8, 2008 Inquirer column surveying three pending 'presidential secrecy' (executive privilege) cases awaiting the Supreme Court as it resumed sessions, and framing them as a test of whether the Court would 'serve or check President Arroyo'

The 'secrecy of conversations' case -- the Senate's motion for reconsideration of Neri v. Senate Committee on Accountability -- and CJP's warning that how the Court rules will shape 'not only the contours of existing jurisprudence but also... the public esteem for the Court,' lest it be derisively branded 'the Arroyo Supreme Court'

The 'secrecy of documents' case -- Roxas v. Ermita, where Senators Roxas and Aquino sought to compel NEDA to surrender the NBN-ZTE meeting minutes -- and the question whether the Court would 'find the courage to enforce the constitutional mandate of transparency and accountability'

The 'secrecy of diplomatic negotiations' case -- Akbayan v. Aquino, seeking disclosure of the JPEPA negotiations -- testing whether 'confidentiality... be validly upheld as an exception to our stringent transparency rule'
sub_topics: The setup: with the Court back from its May break, the public awaited many pending public-interest cases, 'at least three of them' involving presidential secrecy, 'legally known as executive privilege'

Secrecy of conversations -- Neri: the Senate's motion for reconsideration of Neri v. Senate Committee on Accountability (decided March 25, 2008), which had 'sealed the lips' of former NEDA chief Romulo Neri; CJP declines to rehash the merits, stressing instead that the ruling will shape both jurisprudence and 'the public esteem for the Court'

The naming test: quoting his March 30 column, CJP notes that 'an epochal Supreme Court is endearingly named after its chief, like the Davide Court or the Teehankee Court,' but 'when it unduly legitimizes kingly excesses, it is derisively named after the president it serves, like the Marcos Supreme Court' -- hoping the Neri decision is 'a mere aberration' and not enough to brand the present tribunal 'the Arroyo Supreme Court'; the Court must choose, 'to serve or to check President Arroyo,' for 'by its judgment, the tribunal itself will be judged'

Secrecy of documents -- Roxas v. Ermita (GR 180030): Senators Mar Roxas and Noynoy Aquino asked the Court to compel NEDA Director General Augusto Santos (Neri's successor) to submit the minutes and documents behind 'the infamous NBN-ZTE broadband deal'; where Neri shielded a conversation, this petition seeks documents on the same contract

The invocation and the petitioners: Executive Secretary Ermita invoked privilege 'without any justification at all,' not even to the Senate but in a directive to Santos, who used it to snub the Senate's order; the petitioners (through counsels Pacifico Agabin and Jose Anselmo Cadiz) argued the documents were essential 'in intelligently studying' pending bills on infrastructure procurement and foreign loans

The employees speak: the Organization of NEDA Employees (ONE) issued a 'feisty statement' calling for disclosure, lamenting that 'with blind allegiance' they had borne 'the pain of persecution and harassment' under the gag order while 'top management has chosen to keep silent'

The courage question: CJP asks whether the Court will 'find the courage to enforce the constitutional mandate of transparency and accountability for all public officials,' so 'we can proudly continue acclaiming it as the last bastion of democracy'

Secrecy of diplomatic negotiations -- Akbayan v. Aquino: seeking disclosure of the 'behind the scenes' negotiations behind the Japan-Philippines Economic Partnership Agreement (JPEPA), signed by GMA and PM Koizumi in Helsinki on September 9, 2006 but not yet effective for want of Senate concurrence; Akbayan claims the country was disadvantaged, while the government counters that revealing diplomatic secrets would make the Philippines 'a pariah' with whom 'no nation on earth would thenceforth negotiate' -- so 'can confidentiality be validly upheld...? Abangan'

stances.claim: The three pending executive-privilege cases are a defining test of the Court's character: how it rules will shape not just jurisprudence but its 'public esteem,' determining whether it is remembered like the Davide or Teehankee Courts or branded 'the Arroyo Supreme Court' -- for 'by its judgment, the tribunal itself will be judged.'
stances.rhetorical_move: reputation-stakes framing: turning legal cases into a referendum on the Court's identity

stances.claim: The Palace's secrecy claims look weak: in Roxas v. Ermita the Executive Secretary invoked privilege 'without any justification at all,' merely directing a subordinate to snub the Senate -- so the real question is whether the Court will 'find the courage to enforce the constitutional mandate of transparency and accountability.'
stances.rhetorical_move: courage-challenge: reframing the legal question as a test of judicial nerve

stances.claim: The JPEPA case poses a genuinely hard question -- whether 'confidentiality... be validly upheld as an exception to our stringent transparency rule,' given the government's claim that exposing negotiations would make the country 'a pariah' no nation would negotiate with.
stances.rhetorical_move: open-question framing: conceding the diplomatic-secrecy case is closer than the others ('Abangan')

notable_anecdotes: Named after the chief -- or the president: CJP recalls his own line that a great Court is 'named after its chief' (the Davide or Teehankee Court) but a servile one is branded after 'the president it serves,' like 'the Marcos Supreme Court.'
Ermita's bare invocation: he notes that in Roxas v. Ermita the Executive Secretary claimed privilege 'without any justification at all,' merely directing NEDA's Santos to snub the Senate.
The NEDA employees' revolt: he quotes the Organization of NEDA Employees lamenting 'the pain of persecution and harassment' borne under the gag order while management 'chose to keep silent.'

JPEPA's 1,000 pages: he points to the unratified Japan-Philippines treaty -- signed in Helsinki by GMA and Koizumi -- as the test of whether diplomatic confidentiality can survive the transparency rule ('Abangan').

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's June 8, 2008 Inquirer column, previews three pending 'presidential secrecy' (executive privilege) cases as the Supreme Court resumed sessions, framing them as a test of whether it would 'serve or check President Arroyo.' The first, on 'secrecy of conversations,' is the Senate's motion for reconsideration of Neri v. Senate Committee on Accountability, which had 'sealed the lips' of former NEDA chief Romulo Neri; CJP declines to rehash the merits but warns that the ruling will shape both 'the contours of existing jurisprudence' and 'the public esteem for the Court.' Quoting his earlier column, he observes that a great Court is 'endearingly named after its chief, like the Davide Court or the Teehankee Court,' but a servile one 'is derisively named after the president it serves, like the Marcos Supreme Court' -- hoping the Neri ruling is 'a mere aberration' and not enough to brand the present bench 'the Arroyo Supreme Court,' since 'by its judgment, the tribunal itself will be judged.' The second, on 'secrecy of documents,' is Roxas v. Ermita, where Senators Roxas and Aquino sought to compel NEDA's Augusto Santos to surrender the NBN-ZTE meeting minutes; CJP notes Ermita invoked privilege 'without any justification at all,' merely directing Santos to snub the Senate, while the NEDA employees' group (ONE) publicly demanded disclosure -- so the question is whether the Court will 'find the courage to enforce the constitutional mandate of transparency and accountability.' The third, on 'secrecy of diplomatic negotiations,' is Akbayan v. Aquino, seeking disclosure of the JPEPA negotiations (the treaty signed by GMA and PM Koizumi in Helsinki but not yet effective for want of Senate concurrence); here the government warns that exposing negotiations would make the country 'a pariah' no nation would negotiate with -- so CJP leaves genuinely open whether 'confidentiality... be validly upheld as an exception to our stringent transparency rule. Abangan.'
